intro: An amateur actor’s changing voice becomes an exchange between orchestral registers. Oboe and bassoons give the theme a comic, argumentative shape.
question: How does changing register make a melody sound like a character?

sections.label: III · A theatrical voice
sections.mNote: a short Allegretto with contrasting instrumental registers

cues.title: Oboe against lower voices
cues.text: The score gives the oboe a pointed version of the theme and lets bassoons answer from below. Across the variation, compare the high, short gestures with the weight of the lower register.
cues.evidence: Novello p. 15 and Elgar’s commentary identify the oboe and bassoons. Whole-variation listening point; no exact entry is claimed. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Richard Baxter Townshend
cues.text: Richard Baxter Townshend acts an old man in amateur theatricals. Elgar’s portrait recalls a low voice suddenly flying into a higher register: the orchestral contrast comes from a remembered performance.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society identifies Townshend and the amateur theatrical episode. https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm

cues.title: Two swells, one miniature
cues.text: The short variation contains more than one rise in recorded weight. Listen for how a modest phrase can be restated with greater emphasis without becoming a new movement.
cues.evidence: The report has higher-level windows at 0:15–0:20 and 0:45–0:50, separated by quieter music; no literal thematic repeat is asserted from level alone.

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: PDF pp. 15–19, rehearsal figures 8–10, including the repeat and first/second endings on p. 19. The report’s two swells support the repeated traversal; page spans are not a one-way timeline. Desk changes at 0:26, 0:44 and 0:58 remain approximate.

timeline.note: Oboe and low-wind replies contrast above light pizzicato strings; contrabassoon participates in the first gestures (p. 15).
The exchange expands through wind and string figures, acquiring horn and timpani support in the stronger span (pp. 16–17).
The texture becomes lighter, with lower-wind figures and short responses above the strings (p. 18).
The repeated passage brings the string line and wind accents forward again (pp. 16–19, second traversal; the report’s second swell).
Short wind gestures and diminishing strings finish the portrait; horn and timpani support belongs to the cadential span, not every attack (p. 19).

facts: Largely self-taught; violin, organ, orchestral playing and his father’s Worcester music shop
Bandmaster, Worcester County Asylum, Powick, 1879–84 · organist, St George’s Catholic Church, 1885–89 · Master of the King’s Musick, 1924–34
Two completed symphonies; violin and cello concertos; choral works; chamber music; five completed Pomp and Circumstance marches
composer.background:
Elgar learned the orchestra from inside it. His father William kept a music shop in Worcester, tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church. Edward read the scores in the shop, played violin in local ensembles, taught several instruments and eventually succeeded his father at the organ. He was born in Lower Broadheath in 1857, a Catholic in a predominantly Anglican musical establishment and a tradesman’s son in a profession increasingly organised around London colleges. He remained sensitive to both distinctions throughout his later success. His practical education taught him how a phrase feels under a bow.

At Powick he wrote quadrilles and polkas for an unusual ensemble, learning to give each instrument useful work. The Three Choirs Festival brought larger repertory within reach: Handel, Mendelssohn and contemporary oratorio, alongside orchestral music from the Continent. Visits to London widened that education. Wagner mattered particularly: the chromatic connection between chords, the orchestral recollection of earlier events and the long postponement of a cadence all entered Elgar’s language. His mature scores acquired part of their English character through their subsequent public use.
composer.epithet: A Worcester violinist who made orchestral variations into portraits of friends and the concerto into an argument with memory.
